text: You keep a record of scores through a list of operations. An integer records that score. Plus records the sum of the last two scores. D records double the last score. C cancels the last score. Return the total of the record.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Every operation only touches the most recent one or two entries. For example, five, two, C, D, plus: record five and two, cancel the two, double five to get ten, then five plus ten is fifteen. The record is five, ten, fifteen, and the sum is thirty. Can the integers be negative?
Yes, anywhere from minus three times ten to the fourth up to three times ten to the fourth. All operations are valid.

This problem reminds me of a stack. Only the most recent entries matter, last in, first out. I push for an integer, D, or plus, and pop for C. The previous score is always the top. One pass, then sum — linear time and space. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. But how do you read the second-from-top for plus?

With a standard stack I can only see the top. So I pop the top, call it b, read the new top, a, push b back, then push a plus b. A vector used as a stack could index the second-to-last element directly, but the pop-and-restore trick works fine, so I'll stay with the stack.

Here's the plan. One: C pops. Two: D pushes double the top, and plus pushes the top two added together. Three: anything else is an integer, so I push stoi of it. One thing worth flagging — to detect an integer I rule out the three operator strings. Checking is-digit on the first character would miss a leading minus sign.

Alright, let me code this up. It's one loop over the operations with a stack of ints, then a loop that pops everything into the sum. The line to get right is the plus branch: I pop b, peek a, push b back, and only then push a plus b. If I forget to push b back, the record loses a score. The final else catches every integer, negative ones included, since stoi parses the minus sign.

Let's dry-run the code on five, minus two, four, C, D, nine, plus, plus — expected twenty-seven. The row that matters is D right after C: C removes the four, so the top is minus two, and D pushes minus four. Then nine, and the two pluses push five and fourteen. The record is five, minus two, minus four, nine, five, fourteen, which sums to twenty-seven. That matches. It covers negatives, a D on a negative, and back-to-back pluses. And minus two is caught as an integer by the exclude-the-operators check, not by is-digit.
After a C, how does the next D know the right previous score?
The pop makes the top point at the new last entry automatically. Previous is defined as the top, so I never track an index myself. That's why the stack fits so naturally.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — one pass with constant-time push, pop, and top, plus a linear sum at the end. Space is linear for the record stack. The same last-in, first-out idea powers bracket matching, where I match the most recent opener, and postfix expression evaluation, where each operator pops its operands.
Clean. The stack fit, the second-from-top trick, and the integer and negative detection. Done.
